title: I Spent Thirty Years Believing My Worth Was a Number
author: Kelly McGinnis
summary: Kelly McGinnis, a former Fortune 100 executive and president, traces how a childhood on Cape Cod and a college stretch of hiding her background led her to treat her worth as a number she had to prove. She describes two summits ten years apart, financial security and a safe marriage at thirty and a corner-office title in her forties, each of which left her with the same hollow quiet. Her central claim is that the emptiness was not a failure but a message, a form of self-recognition arriving late and telling her that what she was supposed to want was not what she needed. She leaves a marriage and later a title because she finally recognizes the signal. She concludes that real worth lives in agency, the power to choose how to spend her time, and in doing work deep enough to be a legacy. For leaders, the piece is a candid account of how status chasing hollows out judgment and what replaces it.
points: The author spent years hiding her working-class background and building a case for her own existence through relentless work, which shows how insecurity can masquerade as ambition.
Reaching the goals of money, a secure marriage and later a senior title each produced the same hollow feeling, which she reads as information rather than ingratitude.
She argues that the emptiness is self-recognition arriving behind schedule, telling you that your worth was never a number or a title.
Her replacement measure is agency, meaning the ability to choose how to spend your time on work that matters to you and that you would be proud to leave behind.
Walking away twice, from a safe marriage and from a top title, is presented as the first honest choices of real over safe.
quotes: The two emptiest moments of my life were the two times I got everything I wanted.
I was not building a career. I was building a case for my own existence, and I thought if I made it airtight enough, the fear would finally rest.
I had chosen safe over alive and then gone quiet inside the choice, the way you do when a life looks correct on paper.
It was not my life that was hollow anymore. It was the summit itself.
Everything I was supposed to want equated to nothing I actually needed.
The emptiness was never a defect. It was self-recognition, showing up behind schedule, telling me what I didn’t want to hear.

What finally replaced the number was this: my worth lives in agency, the power to choose what I spend my time on, and in doing work so deeply a part of me that it is what I would be proud to leave as my legacy.
